specAnchors.text: know that photographic film or a Geiger−Müller detector can detect ionising radiations
explain the sources of background (ionising) radiation from Earth and space

primer.text: Radiation is invisible, but not undetectable: photographic film darkens where radiation strikes, and the Geiger-Müller tube clicks for every count. Add the ever-present background from radon, cosmic rays and food, and every honest measurement starts by subtracting it.

modules.title: Photographic film and the GM tube
modules.opening: Two detectors cover the syllabus: photographic film, which darkens as it absorbs radiation and so monitors workers’ doses, and the Geiger-Müller tube, which turns each absorbed particle into an electrical pulse and a count rate. Closer to the source, higher the count.
keyPoints: Photographic film detects radiation by darkening when it absorbs it.
Film badges worn by radiographers record cumulative exposure between checks.
The Geiger-Müller tube transmits an electrical pulse for each radiation absorbed.
The count rate rises as the tube moves closer to the source.
The frequency of clicks tracks the intensity of the radiation arriving.

low.restatement: Film is a passive record — wear it, develop it, read the dose. The GM tube is active — it counts every hit with a click, and moving it closer raises the tally.
low.analogy: Film is a sunburn log of your day; the GM tube is a rain gauge ticking with every drop.
low.examPointer: Name the GM tube precisely (Geiger-Müller, GM tube, Geiger counter all accepted); never just "radiation detector".

medium.restatement: Film integrates dose through layered absorbers that discriminate radiation types, while the GM tube resolves counts in real time, so it serves rate measurements and corrected-count work. Distance matters because intensity falls with spreading, so geometry is part of every count comparison.
medium.analogy: Film is the month-end bank statement; the GM tube is the live payment alert on your phone — same information, different time resolution.
medium.examPointer: For "state a detector" questions give both film and GM tube; for rate questions the tube is the answer.

modules.title: Background radiation and its sources
modules.opening: Background radiation is the low-level bath of ionising radiation that surrounds us always. Natural contributors dominate: radon gas seeping from rocks, cosmic rays from space, carbon-14 in living material, and trace radioactivity in food and drink.
keyPoints: Background radiation is the low-level radiation present everywhere, all the time.
Radon gas, an alpha emitter, seeps from rocks and building materials.
Cosmic rays — fast protons from the sun and beyond — strike the atmosphere and produce gamma radiation.
All organic matter carries a trace of carbon-14.
Foods such as bananas carry tiny amounts of potassium-40.

low.restatement: Even with no source on the bench, the counter still ticks: radon from the ground, particles from space, a whisper of carbon-14 and potassium-40 in your lunch.
low.analogy: Background radiation is the faint hiss behind a radio station — always there, usually unnoticed, but real.
low.examPointer: Learn the big three natural sources (radon, cosmic rays, food and drink) — the exam hint names them as the significant contributors.

medium.restatement: Radon matters because it is inhaled — an alpha emitter inside the lungs delivers a large local dose. Cosmic protons spawn secondary gamma in the upper atmosphere, and biological carbon cycling keeps carbon-14 topped up in living tissue, so background dose is a geography-dependent mixture.
medium.analogy: The background is a stew with regional recipes: radon-heavy granite districts, mountain tops with extra cosmic seasoning.
medium.examPointer: Radon is the natural source with the health caveat (inhaled alpha) — pair those two facts if a question asks why radon matters.

modules.title: Corrected count rate
modules.opening: Honest counting subtracts the surroundings: measure the background with no source, then subtract it from every source reading to get the corrected count rate. Artificial sources — medicine, waste, fallout, accidents — add to the natural baseline but repeatable technique keeps them out of your data.
keyPoints: Measure the background count rate with no source present.
The corrected count rate is the source reading minus the background reading.
Repeating readings and averaging, or counting over longer intervals, improves accuracy.
Artificial background sources include nuclear medicine, nuclear waste, fallout and accidents.
A GM tube recording 24 counts per minute of background is 24/60 = 0.4 counts per second.

low.restatement: No source: 24 counts in a minute. With source: 285. Corrected: 285 − 24 = 261 per minute.
low.analogy: Weigh yourself holding the suitcase, then subtract your own weight — only the suitcase remains.
low.examPointer: Show the subtraction line explicitly — "corrected count rate" answers without the arithmetic can drop a mark.

medium.restatement: Because decay is random, a single-minute window is noisy; averaging repeats or extending the interval shrinks the uncertainty on both the background and the source measurements, so the corrected rate inherits the smaller error. Artificial contributions rarely vary over a session, which is what makes subtraction valid.
medium.analogy: Taring a kitchen scale: the bowl’s weight is constant during the bake, so subtracting it once is fair — provided nobody swaps the bowl mid-recipe.
medium.examPointer: If a question offers "repeat and average" as an accuracy improvement, take it — it is the stock answer here.

glossary.definition: The ionising radiation present at all times from natural and artificial sources.
The measured count rate with the background count rate subtracted.
High-speed particles from space that generate secondary radiation in the atmosphere.
A colourless, odourless radioactive gas, an alpha emitter, that seeps from rocks and building materials.

workedExample.prompt: A Geiger counter records 24 counts in one minute with no source present, and 285 counts in one minute with a source present. Find the background rate and the corrected count rate.
steps: Background: 24 counts per minute (24/60 = 0.4 counts per second).
Corrected count rate: 285 − 24 = 261 counts per minute.
In per-second form: 261/60 = 4.35 counts per second.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Background 24 cpm (0.4 cps); corrected count rate 261 cpm (4.35 cps).
